article_units.name: Memory
article_units.subtitle: How memory works as an active process — encoding, storage and retrieval, the multi-store model, reconstructive memory and the factors that distort what we recall.

lessons.title: Processes and Types of Memory
lessons.description: Encoding, storage and retrieval, and the difference between episodic, semantic and procedural memory.
section_markers: how memories are encoded and stored
difference between episodic and procedural memory

lessons.title: The Multi-Store Model of Memory
lessons.description: The sensory, short-term and long-term stores, with the coding, capacity and duration of each.

lessons.title: Serial Position and Murdock's Study
lessons.description: Primacy and recency effects in recall, the serial position curve, and Murdock's classic study of word lists.
section_markers: link of serial position curve to multi-store model

lessons.title: Reconstructive Memory and Accuracy
lessons.description: Bartlett's Theory of Reconstructive Memory, the War of the Ghosts study, and how interference, context and false memories distort recall.
section_markers: Bartlett War of the Ghosts study
factors affecting the accuracy of memory

article_units.name: Perception
article_units.subtitle: How we make sense of what we see — sensation versus perception, depth cues, the nature–nurture debate between Gibson and Gregory, visual illusions and the factors that shape what we perceive.

lessons.title: Sensation, Perception and Depth Cues
lessons.description: The difference between sensation and perception, plus monocular and binocular depth cues that let us judge distance.

lessons.title: Gibson's Direct Theory of Perception
lessons.description: Gibson's nature-based theory that the real world gives us enough information to perceive directly, including the role of motion parallax.
section_markers: strengths and weaknesses of direct theory

lessons.title: Visual Illusions and Gregory's Constructivist Theory
lessons.description: Gregory's nurture-based theory of perception, and explanations for illusions such as the Ponzo, Müller-Lyer, Rubin's vase, the Ames Room, the Kanizsa triangle and the Necker cube.
section_markers: inferences from visual cues and past experience

lessons.title: Factors Affecting Perception
lessons.description: Perceptual set and how culture, motivation, emotion and expectation shape what we perceive. The Gilchrist and Nesberg and Bruner and Minturn studies.
section_markers: Gilchrist and Nesberg study of motivation
Bruner and Minturn study of perceptual set

article_units.name: Development
article_units.subtitle: Early brain development and the nature–nurture debate, Piaget's stages of cognitive development and their use in education, Dweck's mindset theory, and the debate over learning styles.

lessons.title: Early Brain Development
lessons.description: How the brain develops from simple structures in the womb — brain stem, thalamus, cerebellum and cortex — and the roles of nature and nurture.
section_markers: simple neural structures in the womb
roles of nature and nurture in development

lessons.title: Piaget's Theory of Cognitive Development
lessons.description: Assimilation and accommodation and the four stages — sensorimotor, pre-operational, concrete operational and formal operational.

lessons.title: Piaget in Education: Conservation and Egocentrism
lessons.description: Applying Piaget's stages in education, the reduction of egocentricity and the development of conservation. McGarrigle and Donaldson's naughty teddy study and Hughes' policeman doll study.
section_markers: role of Piaget theory in education
McGarrigle and Donaldson naughty teddy study

lessons.title: Mindset, Learning Styles and Willingham
lessons.description: Dweck's Mindset Theory of fixed and growth mindsets, the role of praise and self-efficacy, learning styles for verbalisers and visualisers, and Willingham's criticism of learning styles.
section_markers: evaluation of mindset and learning styles

lessons.title: Hypotheses, Variables and Sampling
lessons.description: Writing null and alternative hypotheses, identifying independent, dependent and extraneous variables, and selecting samples by random, opportunity, systematic and stratified methods.
section_markers: strengths and weaknesses of each sampling method
principles of sampling applied to scientific data

lessons.title: Experimental Methods and Designs
lessons.description: The experimental method and its designs — independent groups, repeated measures and matched pairs — across laboratory, field and natural experiments.

difference between research method and experimental design

lessons.title: Non-Experimental Methods and Correlation

article_units.name: Social Influence
article_units.subtitle: Why we go along with the group and obey authority — conformity and Asch, obedience and Milgram, the authoritarian personality, bystander behaviour and Piliavin, and collective behaviour in crowds.

lessons.title: Conformity and Asch's Study
lessons.description: How social factors such as group size, anonymity and task difficulty, and dispositional factors such as personality and expertise, affect conformity to majority influence. Asch's study of conformity.

lessons.title: Obedience: Milgram and the Authoritarian Personality
lessons.description: Milgram's Agency theory of social factors affecting obedience — agency, authority, culture and proximity — and Adorno's dispositional theory of the Authoritarian Personality.
section_markers: Adorno theory of the Authoritarian Personality
evaluation of agency theory and authoritarian personality

lessons.title: Bystander Behaviour and Piliavin's Study
lessons.description: How social factors (presence of others, cost of helping) and dispositional factors (similarity to victim, expertise) affect bystander intervention. Piliavin's subway study.

lessons.title: Crowd and Collective Behaviour
lessons.description: Prosocial and antisocial behaviour in crowds — how social factors (social loafing, deindividuation, culture) and dispositional factors (personality, morality) affect collective behaviour.
section_markers: evaluation of explanations of collective behaviour

article_units.name: Language, Thought and Communication

lessons.title: Language and Thought

article_units.name: Brain and Neuropsychology

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students conflate the research method (e.g. laboratory experiment, field experiment, observation, questionnaire) with the experimental design (independent groups, repeated measures, matched pairs). The two are distinct decisions a researcher makes: the method is HOW data is gathered; the design is HOW participants are allocated to conditions in an experiment. Examiners report this confusion limits students' ability to answer scenario-based research methods questions accurately.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 examiner report (aqa.org.uk assessment resources) — students 'confused research method with experimental design, which limited their ability to answer questions accurately'.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students mix up the three long-term memory types. Episodic = personally experienced events tied to time and place; semantic = general knowledge and facts; procedural = how to perform learned actions/skills (often without conscious recall). Examiners report students specifically confuse procedural with episodic memory. The spec (3.1.1) names all three and expects students to distinguish them with examples.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 examiner report (aqa.org.uk assessment resources) — 'some students confused procedural memory with episodic memory'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Using the source/stem in application questions
common_misconceptions.misconception: In scenario-based questions students insert their own invented examples instead of identifying and using the information provided in the source text. AO2 application marks are awarded for engaging with the specific scenario, not for generic knowledge. Examiners report students fail to use articles correctly and copy information incorrectly from them.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 examiner report (aqa.org.uk assessment resources) — 'students sometimes fail to use articles correctly, inserting their own examples instead of identifying information from provided text'.

common_misconceptions.misconception: On social influence application tasks students answer the wrong question — e.g. designing a study on bystander behaviour when antisocial behaviour was required, or omitting the dispositional element (personality) when it was specified. The spec (3.2.1) separates social factors from dispositional factors, and the difference between prosocial, antisocial and collective behaviour. Students must read which element the question targets.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 examiner report (aqa.org.uk assessment resources) — 'failure to include the element of personality or designing a study on bystander behaviour rather than anti-social behaviour when required'.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students write hypotheses that are not operationalised — they state a relationship without clearly defining both conditions of the independent variable AND a measurable dependent variable. The mark scheme requires both conditions of the IV and a clear, measurable DV for full marks. A vague prediction ('people will remember better') scores below a precise one ('participants who revise with flashcards will recall more words than those who reread notes').
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 mark scheme guidance (aqa.org.uk assessment resources) — hypothesis questions require 'both conditions of the independent variable and a clear dependent variable which makes the statement operational'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Over-describing and under-evaluating on the extended question
common_misconceptions.misconception: On 9-mark 'describe and evaluate' questions students write pages of description and only a sentence or two of evaluation, capping their mark because AO1 (description) and AO3 (evaluation) are interdependent and a top band needs BOTH developed. The knowledge/description marks are limited; the evaluation carries the rest. Listing evaluation points without elaboration ('it lacked validity' with no reason) does not count as effective evaluation.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 mark scheme and examiner report (aqa.org.uk assessment resources) — on extended responses 'AO1 and AO3 are regarded as interdependent'; students lose marks where 'points listed without elaboration, failing to provide the effective evaluation required for higher mark bands' and where 'additional pages for descriptions but only brief sentences for evaluations'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Justifying conclusions from a study's actual results
common_misconceptions.misconception: When asked to draw or justify a conclusion from a named study, students explain it through outside theory (e.g. cultural differences) instead of pointing to the study's own results. Conclusions must be grounded in what the data of that study actually showed.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 examiner report (aqa.org.uk assessment resources) — 'students often justified conclusions by attempting to explain cultural differences rather than directly addressing the study's results'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Confusing the named studies and theories with each other
common_misconceptions.misconception: Psychology is dense with named core studies and theories, and students mis-attribute them. The spec pairs each named study with a precise topic: Murdock = serial position curve; Bartlett = War of the Ghosts (reconstructive memory); Gilchrist and Nesberg = motivation and perception; Bruner and Minturn = perceptual set; McGarrigle and Donaldson = naughty teddy (conservation); Hughes = policeman doll (egocentrism); Asch = conformity; Milgram = agency theory of obedience; Adorno = authoritarian personality; Piliavin = subway study (bystander); Von Frisch = bee study; Yuki = emoticons; Penfield = interpretive cortex; Tulving = gold memory study; Wiles = effectiveness of CBT; Kaij = twin study of alcohol abuse. Students must attribute each correctly and use it as evidence, never inventing findings.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 specification sections 3.1.1–3.2.4 — each names the specific study/theory paired with its topic (e.g. 3.1.1 'Murdock's serial position curve study', 'Bartlett's War of the Ghosts study'; 3.2.1 'Asch's study of conformity', 'Piliavin's subway study').

common_misconceptions.topic: Treating Gibson and Gregory as the same kind of theory
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students blur the two perception theories. Gibson's direct theory is a NATURE account — the environment provides enough information to perceive directly (bottom-up). Gregory's constructivist theory is a NURTURE account — perception is built from inference, past experience and expectation (top-down), which is why illusions fool us. Each is the named theory the spec uses to frame the nature–nurture debate in perception.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 specification section 3.1.2 — 'Gibson's direct theory of perception – the influence of nature' and 'Gregory's constructivist theory of perception – the influence of nurture'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Ethics treated as a list to name rather than apply
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students name ethical issues (consent, confidentiality, harm) without saying how a researcher would deal with each. The spec explicitly requires 'ways of dealing with each of these issues' as set out in British Psychological Society guidelines — meaning students must pair each issue with a practical solution (e.g. informed consent forms, anonymisation, the right to withdraw, debriefing).
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 specification section 3.1.4 'Ethical considerations' — 'ethical issues in psychological research as outlined in the British Psychological Society guidelines' and 'ways of dealing with each of these issues'.

student_errors_by_question_type.1 mark — Multiple Choice: Students guess without reading all four options. Distractors are written to catch confusion between the named studies, the three memory types, or research method versus design. Eliminate options actively rather than picking the first plausible one.
student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — Define a Term: Students give an example instead of a definition, or define a term using the term itself. A definition needs the meaning in precise psychological language — 'a stratified sample is one where participants are selected in proportion to subgroups in the target population', not 'when you pick a fair mix of people'.
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Describe: Students identify a point but do not develop it. The expected shape is a clear point plus development/clarification. One developed point with correct terminology scores higher than three undeveloped fragments.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Explain or Apply: On application items students answer with textbook knowledge and ignore the scenario; on explain items they describe without explaining the 'why/how'. Marks require either two developed explanatory points or explicit engagement with the stem — name the concept AND link it to the specific situation described.
student_errors_by_question_type.5 marks — Describe a Study: Students give only the findings, or only a vague gist. A full study description covers the aim, method/procedure, results and conclusion of the named study. Findings should be reported as what that study actually showed, never invented or rounded into a generic claim.
student_errors_by_question_type.9 marks — Describe and Evaluate: The highest-tariff item and where most marks are lost. Students over-describe and under-evaluate. AO1 (description) and AO3 (evaluation) are interdependent: a top-band answer needs accurate, detailed description AND clear, elaborated evaluation (each evaluation point developed with a reason — e.g. low ecological validity BECAUSE the task was artificial). Plan the answer as roughly balanced halves and use psychological terminology throughout.

topic_weighting_notes: Two papers, 100 marks each, 50% of GCSE each. Paper 1 = Memory, Perception, Development, Research Methods. Paper 2 = Social Influence, Language Thought and Communication, Brain and Neuropsychology, Psychological Problems. Each paper is split into four 25-mark sections. (Source: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 specification section 2.2.)

AO weighting is AO1 35%, AO2 35%, AO3 30%. Application (AO2) is weighted as heavily as recall (AO1), so scenario practice matters as much as content learning; evaluation (AO3) is nearly a third of the qualification and is mostly earned on the extended 'describe and evaluate' items. (Source: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 specification section 4.2.1.)

Research methods is a discrete Paper 1 topic AND is assessed across all topic areas on BOTH papers via scenario-based questions. Drill research methods application in the context of each topic (e.g. designing a study on conformity, interpreting a correlation about depression), not only as abstract theory. (Source: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 specification sections 2.1, 3.1.4, 3.2 opening notes.)

Named core studies are the backbone of the qualification — roughly sixteen specific studies are named across the eight topics, each paired with a 'describe and evaluate'-able theory. Treat each named study as a discrete revision object (aim, method, results, conclusion, two evaluation points). (Source: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 specification sections 3.1.1–3.2.4 'Additional information' columns naming each study.)

Mathematical and data-handling skills are assessed across both papers, not in a separate section. Students must calculate mean/median/mode/range, interpret tables, bar charts, histograms and scatter diagrams, and understand normal distribution. Computation of statistical-test formulae is NOT required. (Source: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 specification section 3.1.4.1 and Appendix – mathematical requirements; spec states 'Computation of formulae is not required'.)

Therapies and treatments must be evaluated for appropriateness and effectiveness, framed with reductionist and holistic perspectives — this is a recurring AO3 demand in Psychological Problems. (Source: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 specification sections 3.1/3.2 learning outcomes 'evaluate therapies and treatments including in terms of their appropriateness and effectiveness' and 3.2.4 'reductionist and holistic perspectives'.)
current_spec_changes: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 has been taught from September 2017 with first exams in 2019. The current published version is Version 1.1 (14 October 2021) and the specification has been in steady state since. (Source: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 specification cover page 'Version 1.1 14 October 2021'.)

The qualification is linear — all assessment is by two written exams at the end of the course in the same series. There is no coursework or controlled-assessment component. (Source: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 specification sections 2.1, 2.2 and 4.)

Diagnosis of depression and addiction is taught with reference to the International Classification of Diseases as the named diagnostic framework; students should describe diagnosis by number and severity of symptoms rather than reproducing any clinical checklist verbatim. (Source: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 specification section 3.2.4 'The use of International Classification of Diseases in diagnosing unipolar depression' and 'in diagnosing addiction (dependence syndrome)'.)
pedagogical_notes: EEF Cognitive Science in the classroom — retrieval practice is high-value for a study-dense subject. The roughly sixteen named studies and their findings are a finite, drillable set; short frequent low-stakes retrieval (study name → aim/method/results/conclusion → two evaluation points) outperforms massed re-reading. Each lesson ends with a five-question knowledge check for this reason. (Source: EEF blog 'Why bother with retrieval?' and EEF Cognitive Science evidence review.)

EEF Cognitive Science — dual coding suits the biological and structural content. Pair every spatial/structural idea with a labelled visual held in the student's mind: the multi-store model as a left-to-right flow, the nervous system as a branching tree, the brain lobes as a labelled map, synaptic transmission as a sequence. Pair each visual with a one-sentence verbal summary and ask students to reproduce both halves. (Source: EEF Cognitive Science evidence review — dual coding and managing cognitive load.)

EEF Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning (+8 months progress) — explicitly model the structure of the 9-mark 'describe and evaluate' answer before independent practice: balanced description, then elaborated evaluation (each point developed with a reason), then attention to terminology. Students do not balance description and evaluation automatically — examiner reports show they over-describe. Use shared-write worked examples. (Source: EEF Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning guidance report.)

EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools — psychology has dense tier-3 vocabulary (operationalisation, deindividuation, accommodation, agentic state, reductionism). Explicitly teach a focused six-to-eight term glossary per lesson and require precise use; generic synonyms ('forgetting stuff' for interference) cost marks. (Source: EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools guidance report — disciplinary literacy and explicit vocabulary instruction.)

EEF Metacognition — train scenario reading as a metacognitive routine: read the stem twice (once for content, once for the AO2 hooks the examiner has planted), then reference the scenario explicitly in the answer. Examiner reports show application marks are lost when students ignore the source and use invented examples. (Source: EEF Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning guidance report — planning and monitoring strategies applied to curriculum tasks.)

Sensitive-topic handling — Psychological Problems covers depression, addiction and mental health. Present these with care and accuracy as the spec frames them (characteristics of good mental health, lessening of stigma, balanced reductionist/holistic evaluation of therapies), avoiding sensationalism and signposting that the content is educational rather than diagnostic. (Source: AQA GCSE Psychology 8182 specification sections 3.2.4 and 5.7 'Safeguarding'.)
